Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan wrote to me at midnight, and said that we must talk; and I knew in a moment what he meant, for that is a sentence which nobody, I believe, ever speaks as the prelude to any thing agreeable.

We met the next day at a coffee-house in the town. He was already there, and so intent upon what he held in his hand that he did not at first observe me; and he looked nervous. He said that he was not ready for any thing serious, and that the fault was not in me but in himself.

I was not far from tears, but did not cry; I only nodded, and said that it was all right; and then I walked home in the rain, and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

The friend who shared my room thought that I made too much of it; and perhaps I did, but it still gave me pain.

lessons: The chief difference is that your sentences come one short fact at a time, where hers gather a whole turn of the matter into one balanced period and let the narrator's dry judgement fall on it. I joined your first three sentences into 'Ryan wrote to me at midnight... the prelude to any thing agreeable,' and turned his words into reported speech, 'that the fault was not in me but in himself,' so the reader feels the narrator's composure as a kind of irony. Practise joining short sentences with '; and' and 'for,' and understating the strongest feeling, as in 'I was not far from tears,' which works because the refusal to name the tears shows them the more."

faults.quote: I was not far from tears, but did not cry
faults.why: The writer's 'I wanted to cry but I didn't' is a plain wish. 'Not far from tears' shifts it to a physical near-state and softens the degree of feeling a little.

faults.quote: and ate a whole pint of ice cream

faults.quote: Ryan wrote to me at midnight
faults.why: Austen is almost entirely third-person narration, so the first-person memoir narrator is not her natural mode. 'Wrote to me' and 'for that is a sentence which nobody, I believe…' read as Austen in costume more than as her ironic narrator.

faults.quote: cites Emma, ch. 23, ¶ 28

faults.quote: Practise joining short sentences with '; and' and 'for,' and understating the strongest feeling
faults.why: The lesson is thin, with essentially one idea (join sentences, understate). It ends with a stray closing quotation mark. It says nothing about the paragraph 4 verdict or about showing a character's conduct before his speech, which the outline names.

judge.verdict: A competent, mostly faithful Austenian rewrite with a good opening period and sound structure. It adds an unreported incident ('did not at first observe me'), leaves the ice cream anachronism jarring, and its notes are sparse with doubtful citations. The lesson is useful but narrow.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family took possession of the house next door on the Saturday last, and came attended by a cart of uncommon size and by two young children, so that the whole neighbourhood was at once furnished with matter for observation. The father, as far as a first sight could determine, was a very good sort of man; the lady of the party, who was known to be his sister, was rather reserved in her manners than otherwise.

My mother, who never suffered a new neighbour to remain a day without some token of civility, lost no time in carrying them a dish of biscuits. Her object, however, was not mere civility; she meant to learn everything that could be learnt, of the place they came from, of their means of living, and of their going to church.

It soon appeared, however, that the father was a lawyer, and a single man; or, more properly, that he had been married, and was now parted from his wife. My mother, on hearing it, had a look which I understood at once, for I knew exactly what was passing in her mind. She had been trying these many years to see me married; and now, as if on purpose, a single man, and a lawyer, had come to the very door.

The father, as far as a first sight could determine, was a very good sort of man; the lady of the party, who was known to be his sister, was rather reserved in her manners than otherwise.

notes.text: Your second paragraph gives the new family a mother (“The mom is kind of standoffish”), but your last says the father is single and divorced; one household cannot be both. I made the standoffish lady the father's sister, who lives with him and has the care of the children, as Bingley's unmarried sisters live with him in Pride and Prejudice; the narrator knows her for a sister from the first, and the single state of the father remains the discovery.
notes.after: the lady of the party, who was known to be his sister, was rather reserved in her manners than otherwise.

notes.text: The voice frames the arrival through its general effect on the neighbourhood — the very curiosity the passage goes on to show in the narrator's mother.
notes.after: so that the whole neighbourhood was at once furnished with matter for observation

notes.after: Her object, however, was not mere civility; she meant to learn everything that could be learnt, of the place they came from, of their means of living, and of their going to church.

notes.text: The voice gives the mother a standing character in one general clause, so her biscuits read as habit rather than single impulse, and her later motive is the more pointed.

notes.text: The mother's eagerness to marry her child to a single man newly come into the neighbourhood echoes the opening of Pride and Prejudice, and Mrs. Bennet's designs on her daughters. I let the close ring the echo quietly — a single man, and a lawyer, at the very door — rather than copy the sentence itself.
notes.after: She had been trying these many years to see me married; and now, as if on purpose, a single man, and a lawyer, had come to the very door.

notes.text: The narrator's dry aside on the coincidence, saying more than it says: the man's arrival is read through the mother's scheme, which the narrator does not share.
notes.after: as if on purpose

lessons: The chief difference is the sentence: yours run seven or eight words and read like notes, while the author's run near twice a dozen and arrive at their point late. I joined yours into balanced periods \u2014 \u201ccame attended by a cart of uncommon size and by two young children, so that the whole neighbourhood was at once furnished with matter for observation\u201d \u2014 so that each sentence carries a clause of description and a clause of consequence, and the short sentence is saved for a turn. I also let the narrator judge and understate rather than report: the standoffish lady is \u201crather reserved in her manners than otherwise\u201d (litotes), and the mother's scheme is left to land last, where \u201cas if on purpose\u201d says more than it says. Practise naming motive in abstract nouns of judgement (\u201cher object, however, was not mere civility\u201d) and giving feeling by conduct (\u201chad a look which I understood at once\u201d) instead of stating it.

plan.why: The voice opens with the event and its general effect, so that the curiosity the passage goes on to show is already framed as the neighbourhood's, not merely the mother's.

plan.gist: Father and lady judged together in one balanced period.
plan.why: Judgement and litotes in the same breath characterize the family without effusion, and the lady is quietly fixed as a sister so the later discovery does not contradict.

plan.gist: The mother's prompt biscuits, then her true object stated plainly.
plan.why: Civility first, curiosity second, so the irony of her kindness is prepared and the list of her inquiries lands as design.

plan.gist: The discovery, in a period that corrects itself.
plan.why: The single state of the father is the point on which everything turns; the voice lets the sentence amend itself, as gossip does.

faults.quote: who was known to be his sister
faults.why: The sister is invented. The mending is reported, but the draft says "the mom", and the rewrite turns her into a different relation. The mending is defensible, but 'known to be' adds a fact the writer never gave.

faults.quote: so that the whole neighbourhood was at once furnished with matter for observation
faults.why: Adds an event: the whole neighbourhood's reaction. The writer's passage has no such thing. The note calls it a liberty, but it is invented content.

faults.quote: a cart of uncommon size
faults.why: A 'huge truck' becomes a cart, which is an anachronistic substitution. 'Cart' also loses the sense of a moving truck.

faults.quote: It soon appeared, however, that the father was a lawyer
faults.why: 'however' is misplaced and repeated. It already appears in the previous paragraph, and nothing here contrasts with what came before.

faults.quote: now, as if on purpose, a single man, and a lawyer, had come to the very door.
faults.why: Adds the narrator's ironic comment and a 'coincidence' that the draft lacks. The writer's wry reluctance ('I knew exactly what she was thinking') is shifted, and the blunt closing verdict is lost.

faults.quote: a dish of biscuits
faults.why: 'Cookies' becomes 'biscuits', which is acceptable. But the 'right away' urgency is rendered as a general habit ('never suffered a new neighbour to remain a day'), a character trait the writer did not give.

faults.quote: had a look which I understood at once, for I knew exactly what was passing in her mind
faults.why: Redundant: 'understood at once' and 'knew exactly' say the same thing. The sentence is clumsy and un-Austenian in its repetition.

faults.quote: to see me married
faults.why: Fine, but the draft's narrator is an unspecified gender and age. Austen's heroine voice or Mrs. Bennet-like mother ironies are borrowed rather than built. The prose lacks Austen's free indirect discourse.

faults.quote: of their going to church
faults.why: Awkward: 'their going to church' reads stiffly and loses the sense of whether they were churchgoers.

faults.quote: on the Saturday last
faults.why: Odd idiom for 'last weekend'. It is not period-natural and narrows 'weekend' to one day.

faults.quote: as Bingley's unmarried sisters live with him in Pride and Prejudice
faults.why: The comparison is loosely apt but the sisters are in the household for different reasons. The notes also claim a quotation 'cites Sense and Sensibility, ch. 6, ¶ 6' for a sentence that is the rewriter's own, which is a dubious citation.

faults.quote: the mother's scheme is left to land last, where "as if on purpose" says more than it says
faults.why: The 'says more than it says' phrase is a muddled formulation, and the lesson talks of 'near twice a dozen' words, which is vague and rhetorical, not concrete.

faults.quote: or, more properly, that he had been married, and was now parted from his wife
faults.why: Mostly mends 'single, well, divorced', but 'single man' then contradicts 'married' wording: the correction is the draft's own and fine, though 'single' in the last sentence glosses over it.

judge.verdict: A competent Austen pastiche that catches the contradiction in the draft and mends it with a reported sister, but it adds invented content (the neighbourhood, the mother's habit), repeats 'however', and has some stiff or redundant phrasing. The teaching is decent but includes a shaky citation and a vague number.

I've never been to Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

We spent most of the trip at the embassy. He still says it was the best vacation he ever had.
rewrite:
I have never been to Paris; and on the only visit I ever made to it, it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

We spent the greater part of our stay at the consul's office; and he still declares that it was the pleasantest journey he ever made.

rows.text: I have never been to Paris; and on the only visit I ever made to it, it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

notes.text: Your first sentence says you have never been to Paris; your second says 'the last time I was there,' which on the face of it means you have been. I read the second as meaning the one occasion, and wrote 'the only visit I ever made,' so the two agree without altering your meaning.
notes.after: I have never been to Paris; and on the only visit I ever made to it, it rained the whole week
I have never been to Paris; and on the only visit I ever made to it, it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

rows.text: We spent the greater part of our stay at the consul's office; and he still declares that it was the pleasantest journey he ever made.

lessons: The chief difference is that your four short plain sentences become two balanced periods in which the denial is qualified at once and the brother's contrary verdict is reported rather than quoted. The irony does its work in the dry word "still" before "declares that it was the pleasantest journey he ever made," because the narrator's judgement is implied by precision rather than announced. Practise folding a claim and its exception into one period, and letting reported speech carry the joke.

plan.why: the voice does not leave a bare denial standing; she folds the exception into the same breath so the circumstance and the ill-luck close the period.

plan.gist: the stay at the office and the brother's verdict joined with a semicolon, his words reported
plan.why: reporting his speech lets the narrator's dry 'still' carry the whole irony, and the verdict lands last where it tells hardest.

faults.quote: at the consul's office
faults.why: The writer said 'embassy'. A consul's office is a different institution, so a stated fact was changed and the change is not reported.

faults.quote: the pleasantest journey he ever made
faults.why: The writer said 'best vacation'. A journey is not a holiday, and a lost passport plus a week at an office is no 'journey', so the point of the joke shifts.

faults.quote: I have never been to Paris; and on the only visit I ever made to it
faults.why: The contradiction is not mended. 'Never been' and 'the only visit I ever made' still clash in one sentence, and the semicolon makes the clash more glaring. The known fault stays in place.

faults.quote: so the two agree without altering your meaning
faults.why: This claims the mending works, but the rewrite still contradicts itself. The note also does not consider the more plausible readings (a joke, or never having seen Paris beyond the office).

faults.quote: cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 2, ¶ 1
faults.why: The cited paragraph is not an apt model for this balanced period. The move is also credited to a source loosely, as though Austen had written this sentence.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraph 2 changed 'embassy' to 'consul's office' and 'vacation' to 'journey', and none of this is reported.

faults.quote: the brother's contrary verdict is reported rather than quoted
faults.why: The original already reported his words indirectly ('He still says'), so this claimed change did not happen. The lesson also credits the irony to 'still', which the writer already had.

faults.quote: We spent the greater part of our stay
faults.why: This is competent but thin Austen, with little of her characteristic judgement or ironic framing beyond a few formal word swaps ('declares', 'pleasantest').

judge.verdict: The diction is lightly Austenian and the structure is kept, but the central contradiction is left standing while the note claims it was fixed. 'Embassy' became 'consul's office' and 'vacation' became 'journey' without being reported, and the lesson misdescribes what changed.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
And it came to pass at midnight, that Ryan sent word unto me, saying, We must speak together: and I knew straightway what this thing meant.

And on the morrow we met at a coffee shop in the city: and he was there before me, and his eyes were upon his phone; and his countenance was troubled. And he said unto me, I am not ready for a weighty thing: and he said, The fault is not in thee, but it is in me.

And I would have wept, but I wept not: and I inclined my head, and said, It is well: then I went home in the rain, and did eat a whole pot of ice cream.

And the friend that dwelt with me thought that I made more of the matter than was meet: and perhaps it was so; but it grieved me still.

lessons: Your passage is made of short, separate sentences with contractions; the Authorized Version joins clause to clause with 'and' and lets each sentence breathe at twenty words and more, so the one thing flows out of the other instead of being reported piece by piece. Where you wrote 'Ryan texted me at midnight', the voice opens 'And it came to pass at midnight, that Ryan sent word unto me', announcing the turn of the story as it turns; and where you wrote 'I wanted to cry but I didn't', the voice gives the feeling by its sign, 'I would have wept, but I wept not', which carries the withheld grief more plainly than the denial alone. Practise laying clause beside clause with 'and', and giving each feeling by the thing the body does.

faults.quote: and he said, The fault is not in thee, but it is in me.
faults.why: The writer's 'it wasn't me, it was him' is kept, but 'I am not ready for a weighty thing' softens 'something serious' into an odd, vague abstraction; the breakup sense is blurred.

faults.quote: Ryan sent word unto me, saying, We must speak together
faults.why: The writer's 'texted' and 'He said we needed to talk' are conflated, and 'I knew right away what that meant' is kept. 'Sent word' loses the text-message medium, though that is acceptable; the 'He said' is merged into 'saying'.

faults.quote: his eyes were upon his phone; and his countenance was troubled
faults.why: 'Scrolling' is lost, and 'He looked nervous' becomes 'troubled', which shifts the feeling from nervous to distressed.

faults.quote: a whole pot of ice cream
faults.why: The writer wrote 'pint'; 'pot' changes the measure and sounds odd, not Biblical.

faults.quote: And I would have wept, but I wept not
faults.why: 'I wanted to cry but I didn't' is rendered as 'would have wept'; this is an acceptable shift, but 'I wept not' sits awkwardly after 'would have wept' and is a slight loss of 'wanted'.

faults.quote: made more of the matter than was meet
faults.why: 'Overreacting' is rendered in a stilted, near-Elizabethan phrase; 'meet' is used in the KJV, but the whole line feels forced. 'The friend that dwelt with me' is acceptable, though 'roommate' is dropped to a vaguer 'friend'.

faults.quote: and he was there before me
faults.why: The writer says only that he was already there. 'Before me' is idiomatic, but the 'and... and... and' chain in this sentence becomes monotonous.

faults.quote: then I went home in the rain, and did eat
faults.why: 'Then' with colon-spliced clauses breaks the otherwise consistent 'And' pattern; 'did eat' is emphatic-do usage not used in KJV narrative like this.

faults.quote: We must speak together
faults.why: 'Speak together' is slightly unnatural; the KJV would say 'commune' or 'we must talk' in some such form, and 'together' is an invented idiom.

faults.quote: cites 2 Samuel 7:4
faults.why: The citation is for 'and it came to pass that night', which is plausible but is only loosely applicable and unverified; it misses the more usual 'And it came to pass at midnight' (Exodus 12:29) precisely.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “Ryan sent word unto me” — cites Ezekiel 6:1
faults.why: The label lists 'thereof, wherefore' but neither appears in the rewrite; the note is inaccurate about what changed. The citation is also generic.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 3 and 4 have no notes, though they contain the most distinctive changes ('I would have wept, but I wept not', 'meet', 'grieved me still'); the lesson refers to the first of these but the notes do not.

faults.quote: Clauses laid side by side with “and”: “and he was there before me, and his eyes were upon his phone” — cites Zechariah 1:18
faults.why: The cited verse ('Then lifted I up mine eyes') is not a clear example of parataxis with 'and'; the citation is weakly matched.

faults.quote: which carries the withheld grief more plainly than the denial alone
faults.why: The lesson's claim is mostly assertion; 'I would have wept, but I wept not' is hardly a bodily sign but a restated denial, so the 'feeling by its sign' lesson contradicts the example.

faults.quote: And I would have wept, but I wept not: and I inclined my head
faults.why: The writer's short paragraph rhythm is kept, but the rewrite uses colons throughout, which flattens the rhythm; the ending ('but it grieved me still') is kept but the verdict is not shaped to the voice's close.

judge.verdict: A broadly faithful, recognisably Biblical rewrite that keeps the story's order and feeling, but with a few slips ('pot', 'weighty thing', 'speak together'), some strained phrasing, and notes that are thin, partly inaccurate, and missing for the last two paragraphs. The lesson is useful in places but contradicts itself on 'feeling by its sign'.

faults.quote: cites Daniel 4:13

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

rewrite:
Ryan sent me a message at midnight, and he said that we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant, because some messages don't need explaining.

The next day, we met at a diner downtown, and he was already there, looking at his phone. He looked nervous. He told me he wasn't ready for something serious, and he said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry, but I didn't, and I just said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and had a whole carton of ice cream.

rows.text: Ryan sent me a message at midnight, and he said that we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant, because some messages don't need explaining.

notes.text: A gnomic generalization the matter invites: the narrator knew what the message meant without being told, so the voice frames that particular with a general truth, the way he lets one detail speak to a wider truth.
notes.after: because some messages don't need explaining

rows.text: The next day, we met at a diner downtown, and he was already there, looking at his phone. He looked nervous. He told me he wasn't ready for something serious, and he said it wasn't me, it was him.
I wanted to cry, but I didn't, and I just said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and had a whole carton of ice cream.
My roommate thought I was making too much of it, and maybe I was. But it still hurt.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother (“The mom is kind of standoffish”), and your last says the father is single and divorced. A separated father with a live-in wife cannot both be true. I made the standoffish woman the father’s sister, come along with the household — so there is still a woman who keeps to herself, but the father is free to be single, which is the very thing your mother seizes on.

rows.text: I've never really seen Paris. The last time I was there, the rain came down the whole week, my brother lost his travel papers on the second day, and we spent most of the trip at the embassy.

notes.text: Your first line says you've never been to Paris; your second says the last time you were there it rained all week. The two cannot both be true, and the rest of the passage — the embassy, the lost papers, the vacation — shows the trip really happened. I read the first line as meaning you never really saw the city, since the trip you go on to describe was spent at the embassy rather than sightseeing, so the two lines agree.
notes.after: I've never really seen Paris.

notes.text: Obama turns to the listener before the verdict; it frames what follows as the point of the story.
notes.after: Here's the thing

notes.text: the story invites this verdict — the trip went wrong — and Obama's manner states the contrary before the turn, so the landing means more.
notes.after: it wasn't the trip he planned

lessons: The chief difference is that your four flat statements become one accumulating build and one turn: the three troubles are gathered into a single sentence ("the rain came down the whole week, my brother lost his travel papers... and we spent most of the trip at the embassy") so they gain weight together, and the piece lands on an antithesis ("it wasn't the trip he planned, but... the best vacation he ever had") that finds the meaning in what went wrong. faults.quote: he says it was the best vacation he ever had
faults.why: The punchline is kept, but because the preceding clause already adds "wasn't the trip he planned," it explains the irony the writer left implicit.

judge.verdict: The rewrite mends the contradiction and reports it, but it is a thin reshuffle with generic casual phrasing, one added claim ("wasn't the trip he planned"), and a softened "passport." The notes are muddled and cite a dubious source, and the lesson overstates the gains.

yours:
Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan sent me word at midnight, and said we needed to talk, and I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown, and he was already there, fooling with his telephone, and he looked nervous. And then he said he wasn't ready for something serious, and that it wasn't me, it was him—which I judged was his way of saying it was me.

I wanted to cry, but I didn't; I just nodded and said all right, and then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream, which comforted me about as much as the rain did.

My roommate said I was making too much of it, and maybe I was; but it hurt all the same.

rows.text: Ryan sent me word at midnight, and said we needed to talk, and I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown, and he was already there, fooling with his telephone, and he looked nervous. And then he said he wasn't ready for something serious, and that it wasn't me, it was him—which I judged was his way of saying it was me.

notes.text: The voice punctures the old cliché the man leans on, and gives the narrator a wry, unshown reading of what he really meant; the judgment is the passage's own hurt, turned flat.
notes.after: which I judged was his way of saying it was me

rows.text: I wanted to cry, but I didn't; I just nodded and said all right, and then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream, which comforted me about as much as the rain did.

notes.text: A deadpan verdict that the ice cream did not mend anything, left at the end of the sentence so the joke lands and is never explained.
notes.after: which comforted me about as much as the rain did

rows.text: My roommate said I was making too much of it, and maybe I was; but it hurt all the same.

lessons: The chief difference is that your page tells the breakup in short, bare sentences, where Twain would let one clause run into the next on 'and' until it turns on a joke at the very end. Practise the cumulative sentence—'Ryan sent me word at midnight, and said we needed to talk, and I knew right away what that meant'—and the deadpan punch that lands last and is never explained, as in 'which comforted me about as much as the rain did.' The voice stays plain and spoken ('sent me word,' 'all right' in place of 'texted,' 'okay'), because the humor lives in how flatly the thing is said.

outline.gist: Midnight word from Ryan, the request to talk, and what the narrator knows it means.
The coffee-shop meeting: he is there first, nervous, and gives his reasons.
Her stoic reaction: no tears, a nod, a walk in the rain, a pint of ice cream.
The roommate's doubt, her own doubt, and the hurt that stays.

plan.gist: The midnight word, the request to talk, and its meaning.
plan.why: State the plain fact first and let the meaning fall last, where it lands hardest.

plan.gist: The shop, him there first, nervous, then his speech.
plan.why: Set the place and show the man before his words, so the speech comes from a person already seen.

plan.gist: Her understatement, then the deadpan comfort that was none.
plan.why: The stoic 'all right' earns the dry line about the ice cream, which lands the joke and never explains it.

plan.gist: The roommate's doubt, her own doubt, the hurt that remains.
plan.why: The point where it hurts most goes last; the short close lands on the feeling.

faults.quote: which I judged was his way of saying it was me
faults.why: Adds a new interpretation the writer never made. The writer's feeling was plain hurt, and this turns it into a sardonic claim about his motive. It is commentary, but it asserts what he meant.

faults.quote: which comforted me about as much as the rain did
faults.why: Adds a joke that the ice cream failed to comfort. The writer gave no such attitude, and it slightly mocks her own grief. It also implies the rain was a comfort, which contradicts the walk home as misery.

faults.quote: My roommate said I was making too much of it
faults.why: The writer said the roommate 'thought' I was overreacting. 'Said' turns a belief into an utterance, which is a small change of fact.

faults.quote: fooling with his telephone
faults.why: Twain would not have a telephone being fooled with in this modern way. It reads as costume. 'Sent me word' for a text is also an awkward anachronistic blend, since a text is not sent word.

faults.quote: I wanted to cry, but I didn't; I just nodded and said all right
faults.why: This is mostly the original in plain form. There is little Twainian texture such as hyperbole, a vernacular simile, or a digressive aside. Only the 'and' chaining and one joke carry the voice, so it is thin.

faults.quote: And then he said he wasn't ready for something serious, and that it wasn't me, it was him
faults.why: The 'And then... and that' chain is clumsy. The 'and' sequence feels mechanical rather than natural spoken cadence.

faults.quote: Paragraph 1: (no notes)
faults.why: The first paragraph changed several things (texted to 'sent me word', the sentences merged with 'and'), yet no note names them. The same goes for paragraph 4, where 'said' and the semicolon were changed. The notes cover only two liberties.

faults.quote: the judgment is the passage's own hurt, turned flat
faults.why: This claims the added line is the writer's own hurt. In fact it adds a cynical reading the writer did not express, so the note excuses an invention.

faults.quote: The voice stays plain and spoken ('sent me word,' 'all right' in place of 'texted,' 'okay')
faults.why: 'Sent me word' is hardly plain speech. The lesson offers little on Twain's real techniques such as understatement, exaggeration, or the vernacular simile. The outline's reasons are also generic.

judge.verdict: A clean, faithful-ish rewrite with a pleasing chained opening, but the voice is thin, and it adds two inventions (the 'his way of saying it was me' reading and the ice-cream joke) that the notes do not honestly report as additions. The notes miss the smaller changes, and the lesson is only moderately useful.

yours:
A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
The other day a new family moved into the house next door, and they brought a man and a woman and two little children, and a truck so big it looked like it could have moved the house along with the rest of the load. The man seemed nice. The woman, that I took for his wife, was kind of offish.

My mother baked them some cakes right away, and she wanted to find out everything about them—where they came from, what they did for work, and whether they went to church.

It turns out the man is a lawyer, and single. Well, divorced—and the woman, it seems, is his sister. My mother got a look on her face then, and I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to marry me off for years now.

rows.text: The other day a new family moved into the house next door, and they brought a man and a woman and two little children, and a truck so big it looked like it could have moved the house along with the rest of the load. The man seemed nice. The woman, that I took for his wife, was kind of offish.

notes.after: and they brought a man and a woman and two little children, and a truck so big it looked like it could have moved the house along with the rest of the load

notes.text: the writer's 'huge' invites it; the voice sizes the truck into a straight-faced tall-tale image, as a teller of such things would, rather than leaving the bare adjective to do the work.
notes.after: a truck so big it looked like it could have moved the house along with the rest of the load

rows.text: My mother baked them some cakes right away, and she wanted to find out everything about them—where they came from, what they did for work, and whether they went to church.

It turns out the man is a lawyer, and single. Well, divorced—and the woman, it seems, is his sister. My mother got a look on her face then, and I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to marry me off for years now.

notes.text: The draft gives the new family a 'mom' in sentence 4, and then says the dad is single and divorced in sentences 8-9; a wife and a single divorced man cannot both be true of the same household. I made the offish woman his sister, not his wife: the narrator first takes her for the wife, and the discovery corrects that, which agrees with everything else said of her.
notes.after: The woman, that I took for his wife, was kind of offish. ... It turns out the man is a lawyer, and single. Well, divorced—and the woman, it seems, is his sister.

lessons: The chief difference is the telling: the writer's short bare sentences become a narrator talking it through, so the discovery drops deadpan ("Well, divorced—and the woman, it seems, is his sister") and the matchmaking punch line ("trying to marry me off for years now") is left to land last, unexplained. Practise the cumulative "and…and…" sentence for piling up plain facts, and the deadpan correction for the joke: the reader does the laughing, and the narrator never does.

outline.gist: a new family moves in next door, with a truck and two children
the man seems nice, the woman is offish
the mother bakes cakes to find out everything about them
the man is a lawyer, single, divorced
the mother's look, and her years of matchmaking

plan.gist: a new family moves in next door, with a truck and two children
plan.why: name the scene plainly first, and let the truck's size be told flat so the exaggeration sits as fact

plan.gist: the man seems nice, the woman is offish
plan.why: set the nice/offish contrast early, so it pays off when the woman turns out not to be his wife

plan.gist: the mother bakes cakes to find out everything about them
plan.why: the cake-baking is the reconnaissance that produces the discovery, so give it in one run

plan.gist: the man is a lawyer, single, divorced
plan.why: drop the correction deadpan, 'Well, divorced,' and never explain it

plan.gist: the mother's look, and her years of matchmaking
plan.why: save the matchmaking for the last line, where the joke lands and the narrator never laughs

faults.quote: My mother baked them some cakes right away
faults.why: The writer said cookies. Changing the baked good alters a fact and is not reported anywhere in the notes.

faults.quote: The other day a new family moved into the house next door
faults.why: The writer's 'last weekend' is a specific time. Replacing it with a vague phrase drops a detail without comment.

faults.quote: She has been trying to marry me off for years now.
faults.why: The writer's 'set me up' means arranging dates. 'Marry me off' is a stronger claim and shifts the degree of the joke, with no note.

faults.quote: a new family moved into the house next door, and they brought a man and a woman and two little children
faults.why: The 'family' is then said to bring the man, woman and children who make it up. This is redundant and reads as a clumsy attempt at Twain's piling-up.

faults.quote: a truck so big it looked like it could have moved the house along with the rest of the load
faults.why: This is an added hyperbolic image where the writer only said 'huge'. It is reported as a liberty, but it makes the narrator's description go beyond the draft.

faults.quote: My mother baked them some cakes right away, and she wanted to find out everything about them—where they came from, what they did for work, and whether they went to church.
faults.why: This paragraph is nearly the draft unchanged, in modern phrasing ('did for work') with no Twain texture such as dry understatement or a comic gloss. The notes mark it 'no notes', so the voice is applied unevenly.

faults.quote: My mother got a look on her face then, and I knew exactly what she was thinking.
faults.why: This is the draft's modern wording lightly reordered, not Twain's cadence. The closing joke lands flatly and lacks the sly elaboration he would give it.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 21, ¶ 42
faults.why: The paragraph-level citation looks falsely precise and is not clearly apt for this sentence. The notes name only one move, and paragraph 2 and the final sentences get none.

faults.quote: Practise the cumulative "and…and…" sentence for piling up plain facts
faults.why: The lesson is thin and partly generic. It does not explain why Twain's polysyndeton works, and the one example it rests on is awkward in the rewrite.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches and mends the mom/single-dad contradiction and reports it, but it quietly swaps cookies for cakes and drops 'last weekend'. The voice is only lightly Twain, and the opening sentence is clumsy. The notes and lesson are thin.

yours:
I've never been to Paris. The last time I was there it rained the whole week, and my brother lost his passport on the second day.

We spent most of the trip at the embassy. He still says it was the best vacation he ever had.
rewrite:
I never was in Paris but the once, and I judge that was enough; and it rained the whole week we were there, and my brother lost his passport the second day.

We spent most of the trip at the embassy, and he says to this day it was the best vacation he ever had.

rows.text: I never was in Paris but the once, and I judge that was enough; and it rained the whole week we were there, and my brother lost his passport the second day.

notes.text: Your first line says you have never been to Paris, and your very next sentence says you were there; the two cannot both stand. The rain, the embassy, and the lost passport all make the trip real, so I kept the visit and made the first line admit one visit only — 'but the once' — and dropped 'last,' since there was but the one.
notes.after: I never was in Paris but the once, and I judge that was enough; and it rained the whole week we were there, and my brother lost his passport the second day.
I never was in Paris but the once, and I judge that was enough; and it rained the whole week we were there, and my brother lost his passport the second day.
I judge that was enough
notes.cite: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court, ch. 37, ¶ 47

notes.text: the deadpan narrator sizes up his own experience before he tells it; the trip's miseries already point that way, so the voice says it straight instead of leaving it to be inferred.
notes.after: I judge that was enough

rows.text: We spent most of the trip at the embassy, and he says to this day it was the best vacation he ever had.

lessons: Your draft states the facts flat, one after another, with no voice carrying them; Twain's narrator talks it, stringing the miseries into one long run ('I never was in Paris but the once, and I judge that was enough; and it rained...') and letting the brother's verdict fall at the very end where it lands. Practise the deadpan — say the absurd thing straight and never explain it ('he says to this day it was the best vacation he ever had') — and the cumulative sentence that piles 'and...and...' toward a turn, with the punch line last.

outline.gist: never really been to Paris
rain all week, brother's passport lost
stuck at the embassy
brother calls it the best vacation ever

plan.gist: the one visit, and a verdict on it up front
plan.why: the voice sizes up the trip before telling it, so the joke has a rail to run on

plan.gist: rain and the lost passport, piled in one long run
plan.why: a cumulative run lets each misfortune land and keeps the teller sounding like a man talking it over

plan.gist: most of the trip at the embassy
plan.why: the consequence follows the cause, plain, no comment

plan.gist: the brother's verdict, last and flat
plan.why: the deadpan punch lands hardest at the end, and is never explained

faults.quote: and I judge that was enough
faults.why: This is an added opinion that is not in the draft. The note calls it a 'liberty', but it adds a feeling (the trip was unpleasant), and that sits oddly against the brother's 'best vacation' and softens the closing irony.

faults.quote: I never was in Paris but the once
faults.why: The mending is reasonable, but it discards the draft's 'never been' and the possible joke that he never really saw Paris because he was stuck at the embassy. The 'known' note suggests that reading, and the rewrite does not consider it.

faults.quote: I judge that was enough; and it rained the whole week we were there, and my brother lost his passport the second day.
faults.why: The sentence is stitched together with semicolons and 'and's. It sounds like a generic folksy dialect, not Twain's controlled deadpan. 'I judge' is a stock Southern tag, and little else distinguishes the voice.

faults.quote: he says to this day it was the best vacation he ever had
faults.why: This is lightly period-flavored, and the second paragraph is almost unchanged from the draft. There is little Twain texture, such as a concrete exaggeration or a mock-solemn qualifier.

faults.quote: cites Pudd’nhead Wilson, ch. 12, ¶ 1
faults.why: The cited sources are precise-looking but doubtful as exemplars of a cumulative sentence. The paragraph-level citations are unverifiable and probably overconfident.

faults.quote: cites A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court, ch. 37, ¶ 47
faults.why: The 'I judge' aside is attributed to a specific paragraph that does not clearly show the move, so the citation looks fabricated or inapt.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 2:
  (no notes)
faults.why: The second paragraph was changed ('and he says to this day'), but nothing is noted. The note on the first-line fix also says 'dropped last', which is fine, but the change to 'to this day' goes unreported.

faults.quote: Practise the deadpan — say the absurd thing straight and never explain it
faults.why: The lesson claims the rewrite does not explain, yet it inserted 'I judge that was enough', which explains the joke in advance. The lesson therefore contradicts what the rewrite does.

faults.quote: the second day
faults.why: A tiny shift: 'on the second day' became a bare adverbial, which is fine, but 'the whole week we were there' adds 'we', a harmless change.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches and mends the contradiction, but the rewrite adds an opinion ('I judge that was enough') that pre-empts the brother's punchline, and the voice is thin Twain pastiche, with the second paragraph barely changed. The notes' citations look shaky and the lesson contradicts the rewrite's own insertion.
